title: Adaptive headroom estimator, KV thinning, and speculative hedge ladder for OOM resilience
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Goal: Reduce OOM frequency and improve request success rate during peak batching pressure by combining a lightweight GPU headroom estimator, request-level admission scoring that enables targeted KV thinning, and a speculative hedge ladder of micro/quantized fallbacks.

Background: Continuous batching increases effective memory pressure due to wider simultaneous KV residency. Current guards are coarse (global eviction thresholds) which either over-react (high latency degradation) or under-react (OOMs). This ticket designs and implements a request-aware coordination layer that: (1) estimates per-GPU headroom in real time, (2) scores in-flight requests for their memory sensitivity and urgency, (3) performs fine-grained KV segment thinning instead of whole-entry eviction, and (4) applies a speculative fallback ladder (micro-quantized hedge -> quantized base -> CPU-soft-fallback) with bounded retries and jittered backoff.

Approach and components:
- GPU headroom estimator: sample allocator usage + kernel residency windows to produce a smoothed headroom metric (0..1) per device; emits events when headroom crosses soft/hard thresholds.
- Admission controller: request-level scoring based on (prefix-length, expected KV footprint, latency SLO, user tier). Uses score to decide: accept, accept-with-kv-thin, defer-to-hedge, or reject.
- KV thinning: represent KV entries as scored segments (recent tokens first). Thinning evicts lower-score segments preferentially; retains high-value prefixes. This is cooperative (both serving runtime and cache manager participate) to avoid wide ripples in batch scheduling.
- Speculative hedge ladder: if admission decides insufficient headroom, attempt hedging paths in order: (a) micro-model — tiny distillation/4-bit quant with reduced context (fast, small memory), (b) quantized base model with prefix trimming, (c) CPU-serve soft-path with increased latency but preserved completion. Each hop has bounded retry budget and deterministic fallback ordering.
- Backoff & retry policy: controlled exponential backoff with randomized jitter; hedges launched as parallel speculative attempts only for high-urgency requests to limit cost.
- Telemetry & SLOs: new metrics (headroom_smoothed, kv_thin_rate, hedges_launched, hedge_success_rate, oom_count_per_gpu) and dashboards. Define targets: reduce OOM count by 80% on 99th-percentile load spikes; maintain P99 latency within 1.4x baseline for critical tier.

Design trade-offs considered:
- Precision vs. overhead: headroom estimator samples every X ms; we chose a 200ms default to balance reactivity and CPU overhead.
- KV thinning granularity: segment-based trimming adds metadata costs; we limit segment count per entry to cap overhead.
- Speculative cost: hedges can double cost for hedged requests; we restrict hedges to high-urgency and to a global concurrency budget.

Acceptance criteria:
1) Headroom estimator deployed with unit+integration tests and a working grafana panel.
2) Admission controller correctly flags and routes requests in synthetic stress tests (oom-inducing rehearsal) with deterministic behavior.
3) KV thinning reduces global eviction tail variance vs baseline in perf benchmarks.
4) End-to-end canary: during a controlled spike, OOMs drop >= 80% and critical P99 latency remains <= 1.4x baseline.
5) PRs merged and rollout guide written (runtime/README + runbook entries).

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: over-thinning harms quality. Mitigation: conservative initial thinning fraction and per-customer quality monitors; rollback flag in console.
- Risk: estimator false positives cause unnecessary fallbacks. Mitigation: require 2 consecutive threshold crossings and attach short grace window.

Next steps:
1) Prototype headroom estimator (ENG spike measurement harness) — Diego (in progress).
2) Implement KV segment metadata and thinning operations (work item).
3) Wire admission controller and hedging ladder, add telemetry.
4) Run chaotic stress tests and iterate.
